story.headline: Low-Calorie Diet Puts 54% of Young Adults Into Type 2 Diabetes Remission
story.summary: Low-Calorie Diet Puts 54% of Young Adults Into Type 2 Diabetes Remission

carousel.cover_headline:
A Diet Change Put
54% of Young Adults
Into Diabetes Remission.

slides.label: THE STUDY
slides.headline: 96 young adults with type 2 diabetes joined a strict trial.
slides.insight: Half followed a low-calorie diet and exercise. Half received standard care.

slides.label: THE RESULT
slides.headline: **54%** in the diet group reached remission after 24 weeks.
slides.insight: In the standard care group, only about 4% reached remission.

slides.label: HOW THEY DID IT
slides.headline: 800–900 calories daily, plus protein, fruit and vegetables.
slides.insight: Supervised exercise twice a week was also part of the programme.

slides.label: WHAT REMISSION MEANS
slides.headline: Remission meant normal blood sugar, no glucose-lowering medication.
slides.insight: Measured at 24 weeks; long-term outcomes need further research.

slides.label: TRY THIS WEEK
slides.headline: Add one portion of fruit and two of non-starchy vegetables daily.
slides.insight: Small, consistent food changes are where real health shifts begin.

sources: RESET for Remission randomized trial, McGill University and University of Leicester, 2026 (reported by Global Agriculture, published in The Lancet Regional Health, Americas, presented at European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meeting)
carousel.caption:
A diet change put 54% of young adults into diabetes remission.

A supervised low-calorie diet and exercise programme put more than half of 96 young adults (aged 18–45) with early-onset type 2 diabetes into remission after 24 weeks, compared with about 4% who received standard care — according to the RESET for Remission trial run in Canada and the UK.

This was a structured clinical trial, not a quick fix. But it shows that food and movement are powerful. What would it take for your family to eat one more portion of vegetables today?

Not medical advice.

Sources: RESET for Remission trial, McGill University and University of Leicester, 2026 (The Lancet Regional Health, Americas; reported by Global Agriculture)
